Florence Cathedral, formally Santa Maria del Fiore and colloquially called the Duomo, is a masterpiece of Italian Gothic and early Renaissance architecture located in Florence, Italy. Construction began in 1296 and was completed in 1469. Its most iconic feature is Filippo Brunelleschi's revolutionary dome, completed in 1436, an engineering marvel that crowned the vast octagonal lantern. The cathedral was a symbol of Florence's civic pride and mercantile wealth, attracting the Renaissance's greatest sculptors and architects and serving as the setting for major religious and civic ceremonies.

The cathedral was designed by Arnolfo di Cambio in 1296 as a symbol of Florence's growing power and wealth. Its vast size was ambitious, and the empty space above the octagonal crossing was so wide that architects had no solution for covering it for over a century. Filippo Brunelleschi resolved the dome problem in 1419 with an ingenious double-shell construction using herringbone-patterned brick, revolutionary at the time. The dome has no supporting internal framework and remains a triumph of engineering and geometry.

The cathedral's facade is clad in polychrome marble in white, green, and pink, creating a striking geometric pattern. The original facade was partially completed by Giotto in 1334 and later completed in the nineteenth century. Giotto's Campanile, the bell tower adjoining the cathedral, is a freestanding tower of distinctive geometric marble bands. Designed by Giotto and completed by Andrea Pisano, it is one of Florence's most recognizable monuments.

The cathedral's interior was a canvas for Renaissance artists. Dante Alighieri, author of the Divine Comedy, was honored with a monument inside. Frescoes by Paolo Uccello and Andrea del Castagno adorn the walls. The cathedral was the site of major Renaissance ceremonies including the coronation of popes, the beatification of saints, and celebrations of military victories. It was the spiritual and symbolic heart of Florence. The bronze doors created by Ghiberti and others are masterpieces of Renaissance sculpture. Ghiberti's north doors, completed in 1452, depict biblical scenes with unprecedented realism and perspective, influencing Renaissance art profoundly.
